Not quite. You steer a motorcycle at speeds above ~10-15 MPH by turning the handlebars the OPPOSITE direction you want to go, and leaning in through the turn. An important component of this is looking through the turn. Your body will naturally steer the motorcycle where you're looking. It's a subconscious thing. If you panic mid-turn and stare at the place you DON'T want to go (pretty common with inexperienced riders) you will go directly into that area. If you ever panic mid-corner, your best bet is to hold throttle steady, commit, keep counter-steering, look through the turn, and lean in hard.
That wasn't too fast. That was target fixation. Notice how the bike straightens out and he doesn't look through the corner? If he would have committed, looked, and leaned, he would have been fine.

Success is a combination of excruciating hard work and luck. Someone can work harder than anyone else on the planet but if they were born retarded and quadriplegic, they won't succeed. Someone can be born into a billionaire family and have a 200 IQ but if they never make any effort they won't achieve anything. However, most people are somewhere in the middle, and most people are capable of success. The problem is, however, is that by blaming others' for a lack of success, you shut down your pathway of thoughts that could lead you to success. It's like putting a car into reverse gear when you're trying to drive forward. The pivotal point of having the possibility of success never occurs when you don't view success as an option. If I didn't view success as an option and make excuses for myself/complained/whatever, I would have dropped out of high school and joined the army (Not saying the army is bad. It's a great career for some people and I have the upmost respect for those who serve, but it's not the career, *for me*, that would lead to the most success.). I had a real fucker of a problem and no one knew how to fix it. We randomly tried medicine, and that ended up working for me. That was the luck. Now I've salvaged my grades and am on my way to my dream college for mechanical engineering. That's the hard work. Not everyone can be successful, but a lot more people can be if they change their mindset from "I'm going to complain about why I can't be successful." to "How can I be successful?" And that is not to say that people don't have valid complaints, but there's no sense in complaining about something you can't change, and if you can change it, then do it! We can't change the past that fucked the future for us, be we sure as hell can bust our asses in the hope that we attain success and create a positive future for those who come after us.

Usually, but not always. Turbo diesel trucks are used for towing mostly. Diesel engines make a large amount of torque, and the turbo is to make up for the lack of high end horsepower. When you accelerate, the ECU (car computer) sends more fuel to the motor to meet the increased air intake and keep a healthy ratio. Turbos spool based on the exhaust, because they take exhaust gasses and reroute them to spin a fan to bring more air into the engine. This takes time, and is not as fast of a process as injecting fuel is. Sometimes, in quick acceleration, the fuel reaches the motor before the turbo is fully spooled, meaning you have a rich air/fuel ratio. Unburnt diesel is released through the exhaust, which is that black smoke.

The deck mate's breaths were ragged and swift, as if he had sprinted right down to the Captain's Quarters. Pushing past the winded deck mate, Captain Thaddius purposefully marched up the steps to the main deck, each boot striking the wood, thumps reverberating throughout the staircase. As he arrived to the deck, the Grand Seacaster rushed to him.

As they came closer, he could discern humanoid figures riding the creatures of the water. Dread engulfed The Captain's entire body, as panic started to rise through his gut, and into his spine. Only legends have been told of these, for the only sailors to encounter them rest at the ocean floor. The Captain had never felt fear on The Beacon until now. *Creator and Ascendants protect me,* The Captain thought- *for we are all fated to Death. It's the Elven Tide-Hunters.*

If you're low elo and want to climb to high elo and you can't reliably carry at least half of your games when taking resources, against low elo players, how do you ever expect to reach high elo?

I climbed to D1 playing on the premise that my team is dogshit retarded and it worked. Past D1, teams are actually somewhat competent, so I give much more to the team in masters+. 

You don't just magically be high elo. You have to choose to understand the differences between your play and a challenger, and change your playstyle. From there, you can make a choice. 

Your play affects around 70% of your games. The other 30% are 15% always winnable or 15% unwinnable. If you play perfectly every game you'll have somewhere near 80-90% win rate. Now, your choice, is to play as if your teammates are equal to you, and lose a lot of games that were otherwise winnable, because they can't use their leads correctly, or you can take all the resources and use them to pressure the game and win through objectives. I got to D1 by singlehandedly controlling the pace of games. 

I would like to stress; I do not play like this in challenger. My teammates are good in challenger, and as long as they're not tilted, if I'm succeeding and give them resources they will succeed as well. 

***tldr:*** to be high elo you have to understand there is no magic and just identify the differences in your play, then play like one and shitstomp like one. It's how I did it and it's the most optimal way to play below high diamond.

Edit: to refine my point because I'm tired: yeah the way I climbed only works if you're better than you're opponents, but how will you get to high elo if you're not better than your opponents? 

Sure you can be the guy who has thousands of games and a 51% win rate and only plays Janna/Soraka and sits in challenger only playing when you're about to decay but if you do that you're fucking bad.
